# The Groove: How a Vinyl Record Is Made, Pressed, Played and Collected

> A cited, independent field guide to the vinyl record: cutting the lacquer, plating and pressing, sizes and speeds, what the runout etchings mean, turntables and DJs, collecting and grading, what a record costs, and where records are made. With a runout decoder.

Independent cited field guide, 28,923 words, 200 sources, updated November 2026. Not affiliated with any label, plant, store or brand.

## Sections
- [A short history of the record](https://groove.cold.fyi/history/): The record went from tinfoil cylinders in 1877 to shellac 78s to Columbia's vinyl LP in 1948 and RCA's 45 in 1949, which split the market into albums and singles. Cassettes and then CDs pushed vinyl to a rounding error by the mid-2000s. Since then US vinyl has grown 19 years in a row, passing $1 billion in revenue in 2025.
- [How a record is cut](https://groove.cold.fyi/cutting/): Every pressed record starts as a groove carved in real time by a heated stylus on a lathe, usually into a lacquer-coated aluminum disc, one side at a time. The cut obeys physics a streaming master never meets: bass has to stay centered, harsh "s" sounds have to be tamed, and every extra minute on a side costs level, bass or both. The machines are mostly decades old, with a couple of new ones arriving since 2023, and the playback curve that undoes the cutting EQ has been standard since 1954.
- [How a record is pressed](https://groove.cold.fyi/pressing/): A pressed record is a copy of a copy of a copy. The cut lacquer is silvered like a mirror, grown into nickel negatives and positives in a plating bath, and the last generation, the stamper, is mounted in a press that squeezes a warm lump of PVC at something like 100 tons for about half a minute. Many plants keep old presses running on salvaged parts, the compound and lacquer supply has hung on very few suppliers, and the 2020 fire at a California lacquer plant plus a demand surge produced waits of up to 10 months. By early 2025 typical backlogs were down to about three months.
- [Sizes, speeds, weights and colors](https://groove.cold.fyi/formats/): A 12 inch at 33 1/3 rpm holds about 18 to 22 minutes a side, more if the music is quiet; spin the same disc at 45 and you trade minutes for a faster groove. A 180 gram record is pressed from the same stampers, with the same groove depth, as a standard one of about 140 grams, and the people who build turntables can't agree on whether the extra weight does anything for the sound. Colored, splatter and picture discs are made differently from black and can be noisier, and the new PET "eco" records arrive with claims that only their makers have tested.
- [The runout groove: what the etchings mean](https://groove.cold.fyi/runout/): The smooth band between the last song and the label is called the **dead wax** or runout, and it carries the record's paperwork: a matrix number for each side, cut numbers, stamper codes, plant marks and often the initials of the engineer who cut it. Read the right way, those scratches can tell you which factory pressed your copy and which lacquer it came from, but no single mark proves a first pressing on its own. And every so often there is a joke in there too.
- [How a turntable plays a record](https://groove.cold.fyi/playing/): A diamond the size of a grain of sand rides a wiggling groove, and a magnet and a coil turn that wiggle into a tiny signal that a phono preamp lifts and corrects. Most skips, hiss, lopsided stereo and worn records come down to a few settings and storage habits. Playing a record does wear it, though the two classic lab studies disagree about what happens to the groove.
- [Records and DJs](https://groove.cold.fyi/dj/): DJs turned the record player into an instrument. A Japanese direct-drive turntable launched in 1972 became the club standard, scratching came out of the Bronx in the mid-1970s (exactly when, and who was first, is still argued), and since the early 2000s timecode vinyl has let DJs keep a record under their hand while playing digital files.
- [Collecting and grading records](https://groove.cold.fyi/collecting/): Collectors chase first pressings, but the codes in the dead wax only get you part of the way, and collectors can't even agree on what counts as a "second pressing". Condition is graded on a shared ladder from Mint to Poor: the Goldmine scale in the US and on Discogs, the Record Collector scale in the UK. Discogs users added 114.2 million items to their collections in 2025, a company record, and Record Store Day has run every year since 2008.
- [What a record costs, and who gets paid](https://groove.cold.fyi/money/): Pressing costs a few dollars a record at 1,000 copies and $10 or more at 100, because setup costs land on every run whatever its size. Sell the result for $24 in an indie shop and, in one label's breakdown, the label and the artist each keep about $3.19. US vinyl revenue passed $1 billion in 2025 for the first time since 1983.
- [Vinyl and the planet](https://groove.cold.fyi/planet/): Most records are pressed from **PVC** (polyvinyl chloride), a petroleum-based plastic. Kyle Devine of the University of Oslo estimates the US recording industry used far less plastic in 2016 than at the vinyl peak of 1977, but produced more greenhouse gas, because storing and streaming digital files takes energy too. Makers are trying bio-based PVC, bioplastics and injection molding; the gains they report are their own claims, not independent measurements.
- [Where records are made](https://groove.cold.fyi/world/): The world's biggest presser sits in a small town near Prague: GZ Media, which pressed more than 55 million records in 2021 and runs plants on two continents. North America went from about 15 plants in 2014 to a projected 43 in the US alone by 2022, while Japan still had at least one fully functioning plant in 2010 and Brazil had a second plant on the way in 2016.
- [Test yourself, and where to go next](https://groove.cold.fyi/next/): A quiz covering every chapter, the glossary, the best outside reading, and the questions nobody has answered in public yet. If you can answer one with a source, the corrections desk wants to hear from you.
